"I was writing." Berenguera turned the report face down. "Your clerk. How is his thumb?"

"White to the knuckle and no further. He told me today what he would not say in the hall." Azalais's mouth twisted. "Montclar clerks swear at their indenture to set their thumb only to words that can be kept. He doubted the road clause as he copied it, and pressed anyway, because the prince's men were watching."

So it had never been the initial. It had been the wavering. Berenguera felt the last loose knot of the thing pull tight.

Berenguera answered carefully, as a notary. "A promise heard with terms binds, even without seal. The death of the other party does not release the living. That is our law."

"Even if I misunderstood?"

"Intent is read from words spoken, not wishes after."

Azalais was quiet. She advanced a rook. "Then I am bound to try the marriage."

Berenguera remembered the first night at Greyhook House, rain needling the shutters, Azalais resetting the pieces after beating her in eleven moves and laughing through her nose.

"You play like a notary," Azalais had said, turning the cedar queen in her fingers. "All defense. Tell me, as a notary. If I promised my mother on her deathbed that I would make this marriage work, and the marriage itself is a trap, does it still count?"

"The dead cannot release an oath," Berenguera had said. "But the living can read the terms narrow. What did you promise, word for word?"

"To make the peace hold." Azalais had set the queen down hard. "Not to marry. I only thought they were the same."

They were not the same. Berenguera had seen that clearly when she found the yellow draft in Guilhem's rooms, the hollow clause in his neat hand, the margin note in pencil, One night's silence, love. She had refused him. She had kept the draft.
